appraisal_events.evidence: Bergotte: « Mais c'est un vieux serin »; Mme Swann: « il est ennuyeux comme la pluie », « je l'ai trouvé d'un vaseux »; Bergotte again on « la provision de sottises qui empèsent le jabot de la chemise »; and the narrator's own verdict: « Les arguments de M. de Norpois (en matière d'art) étaient sans réplique parce qu'ils étaient sans réalité. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The whole conversational scene converges on ridiculing Norpois, and the narrator's essayistic aside ratifies the mockery by declaring his authority empty rather than merely unpleasant; even Swann's ostensible defense reduces him to a curiosity as a lover.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Cela ne prouve pas que les opinions de Bergotte fussent moins valables que celles de l'Ambassadeur, au contraire. Une idée forte communique un peu de sa force au contradicteur »; Mme Swann « avait grande confiance dans le jugement de Bergotte ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly rates Bergotte above Norpois: his disagreement is fertile because his ideas are real, and the hostess defers to his judgment, so his rhetorical and intellectual standing rises in the same movement that lowers the Ambassador.

status_effects.explanation: Every voice in the room, and the narrator behind them, treats Norpois as tedious, stale, and malicious; he ends the passage labelled « très mauvaise langue ».
His unanswerable authority is re-described as an absence of substance, so the silence he imposes counts against him rather than for him.
Bergotte's contradiction is presented as strengthening his interlocutor, making the final judgment a joint work; this is the passage's model of real intellectual force.
He is locally raised as the trusted arbiter of the salon and as the antithesis of Norpois's hollow authority.

ambiguities: Swann's local movement is genuinely mixed and is therefore not recorded as a dominant event: the narrator exposes his petty vanity (« même chez les êtres supérieurs [...] l'amour-propre reste mesquin ») and shadows him with the Racine/Louis XIV disgrace anecdote, yet also grants his maxim on jealousy « la valeur d'un avertissement prophétique », so the passage neither clearly lowers nor raises him.

Mme Swann's compliment on Bergotte's opuscule is ironized by the narrator (she praises it « pour faire croire qu'elle avait lu la brochure » and in order to direct him), so it functions less as praise of Bergotte than as exposure of her hostessing; the narrator then partly reverses this by conceding « elle l'inspira, d'une autre façon », leaving her own standing undetermined.
